module_title: Fundamental Rights, Duties, and DPSPs: Foundational Concepts
introduction: This foundational level introduces the core constitutional triad that governs the relationship between the State and the Citizen. It defines the 'Magna Carta' of India (Fundamental Rights), the blueprint for a Welfare State (DPSPs), and the moral obligations of the citizens (Fundamental Duties).

core_concepts.title: Fundamental Rights (FRs) - Part III
core_concepts.description:
Enshrined in Part III (Articles 12-35) of the Constitution. 
- Source: Inspired by the US Bill of Rights.
- Nature: They are 'Justiciable' (legally enforceable in courts). If the State violates them, a citizen can directly move the Supreme Court (Art 32) or High Court (Art 226).
- Purpose: To promote political democracy and prevent authoritarian rule. They act as limitations on the tyranny of the executive and arbitrary laws of the legislature.

core_concepts.title: The Six Fundamental Rights
core_concepts.description:
Originally there were 7, but the Right to Property (Art 31) was removed by the 44th Amendment (1978) and made a legal right (Art 300A).
1. Right to Equality (Arts 14-18)
2. Right to Freedom (Arts 19-22)
3. Right against Exploitation (Arts 23-24)
4. Right to Freedom of Religion (Arts 25-28)
5. Cultural and Educational Rights (Arts 29-30)
6. Right to Constitutional Remedies (Art 32)

core_concepts.title: Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSPs) - Part IV
core_concepts.description:
Enshrined in Part IV (Articles 36-51).
- Source: Borrowed from the Irish Constitution (which borrowed it from the Spanish Constitution).
- Nature: They are 'Non-Justiciable' (cannot be enforced by courts if the State fails to implement them).
- Purpose: To establish social and economic democracy. They act as guidelines/instructions to the State to build a 'Welfare State' rather than a 'Police State'.

core_concepts.title: Fundamental Duties (FDs) - Part IVA
core_concepts.description:
Enshrined in Part IVA (Article 51A). Not present in the original Constitution.
- Origin: Added by the 42nd Amendment Act (1976) on the recommendation of the Swaran Singh Committee. Inspired by the USSR Constitution.
- Count: Originally 10; the 11th duty (education for children aged 6-14) was added by the 86th Amendment (2002).
- Nature: Non-justiciable moral and civic obligations of citizens.

important_entities.name: Definition of 'State' (Article 12)
important_entities.key_fact: Fundamental Rights are primarily claimed against the 'State'.
important_entities.significance: Before claiming an FR violation, one must prove the violator is the 'State'. Article 12 defines State to include the Government and Parliament of India, State Governments/Legislatures, all local authorities (municipalities, panchayats), and 'other authorities' (like LIC, ONGC, SAIL) functioning under the control of the Government of India.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation:
Examiners frequently test which rights are for citizens vs. foreigners. 
- Available ONLY to Citizens: Articles 15, 16, 19, 29, 30. 
- Available to BOTH Citizens and Foreigners (except enemy aliens): Articles 14, 20, 21, 21A, 22, 23, 24, 25, 26, 27, 28.

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Memorize this sequence like a phone number. These 5 articles are strictly reserved for Indian citizens (protecting against discrimination, public employment, 6 freedoms, and minority cultural rights).

exam_strategy_tips: Whenever a question asks 'Which part of the Constitution deals with the concept of a Welfare State?', the answer is always **Part IV (DPSPs)**.
